가상자산(암호화폐) 시장에서 불마켓(강세장)의 시작과 진행을 알리는 대표적인 핵심 매수 신호 15가지  1. 기술적 분석 & 차트 신호  1. 골든크로스 발생  주요 이동평균선(예: 50일 이동평균선)이 장기 이동평균선(예: 200일 이동평균선)을 아래에서 위로 뚫고 올라가는 전형적인 상승 전환 신호입니다.  2. 주요 저항선 돌파 및 지지 확인  수개월 또는 수년간 넘어서지 못했던 강력한 가격 저항선을 거래량을 동반해 돌파한 후, 해당 가격대가 새로운 지지선으로 자리 잡는 현상입니다.  3. 상대강도지수(RSI) 및 지표 상승 전환  RSI, MACD 등의 기술적 지표에서 주가는 하락하는데 지표는 상승하는 '강세 다이버전스(Bullish Divergence)'가 발생하거나, 장기 추세선 상단으로 지속 진입합니다.  4. 거래량을 동반한 장대양봉  바닥권이나 박스권 상단에서 평소 거래량의 수배에 달하는 대량 거래량과 함께 강력한 장대양봉이 출현합니다.  2. 온체인(On-Chain) 데이터 신호  5. 거래소 보유 물량 감소 (지갑 유출 증가)  중앙화 거래소(CEX)의 코인 잔고가 지속적으로 줄어들고, 투자자들의 개인지갑(하드월렛 등)으로 이동하는 현상으로 장기 보유 의지를 나타냅니다.  6. 채굴자 세력의 판매 중단 및 매수 전환  채굴자들의 코인 이동량이 줄어들고, 채굴 비용 대비 수익성을 나타내는 Hashribbons 지표 등에서 매수 신호(Buy Signal)가 포착됩니다.  7. 장기 보유자(HODLer) 공급량 최고치  1년 이상 코인을 이동시키지 않은 장기 투자자들의 보유 비중이 역사적 신고점을 기록하며 시중 유통 물량이 잠기는 현상입니다.  8. 스테이블코인 공급량(발행량) 증가  USDT, USDC 등 스테이블코인의 총발행량이 급증하고 거래소 유입이 늘어나며, 시장에 매수 대기 자금이 풍부해집니다.  3. 시장 구조 & 매커니즘 신호  9. 비트코인 도미넌스(시가총액 점유율)의 변화  상승 초기에는 비트코인 점유율이 먼저 급격히 상승하며 시장을 이끌고, 이후 점유율이 하락하며 알트코인 급등장(알트불장)으로 자금이 순환됩니다.  10. 선물 펀딩비(Funding Rate)의 양수 지속  무기한 선물 시장에서 롱(매수) 포지션 비율이 우위를 점하며 펀딩비가 지속적으로 플러스(+)를 유지합니다.  11. 미결제약정(Open Interest)의 완만한 증가  선물/옵션 시장에서 가격 상승과 함께 미결제약정이 안정적으로 증가하며 강한 추세를 뒷받침합니다.  4. 거시경제 & 대외적 환경 신호  12. 글로벌 완화적 통화정책 (금리 인하 및 유동성 공급)  미국 연준(Fed) 등 주요국 중앙은행이 금리를 인하하거나 자산 매입을 통해 시장에 달러 유동성을 푸는 시기입니다.  13. 제도권 자금 유입 (ETF 승인 및 기관 매수)  비트코인/이더리움 현물 ETF로의 지속적인 순유입 또는 글로벌 대형 기관/기업들의 재무제표 자산 편입 소식이 이어집니다.  5. 심리 & 대중 관심도 신호  14. 구글 트렌드 및 SNS 검색량 증가  '비트코인', '코인' 등 관련 키워드의 구글 검색량과 X(구 트위터), 유튜브 등 SNS 언급량이 계단식으로 상승합니다.  15. 공포·탐욕 지수(Fear 일평 미국주식 전날 마감시황(26.10.23)   한눈에 보기  목요일 나스닥을 2.6% 끌어내렸던 AI 투매가 금요일에는 모양을 바꿔 시장 전체로 번졌다. 기술주 자체는 반등을 시도하며 선방했지만, 이번에는 금융·경기민감주·방어주까지 두루 팔리면서 다우가 650포인트 넘게 밀렸다. 다우존스 산업평균지수는 1.2% 하락한 52,215선, S&P500은 0.5% 내린 7,624선, 나스닥 종합지수는 0.2% 하락한 25,955선에서 마감했다. 러셀2000도 0.3% 내린 2,776선으로 소형주 역시 피하지 못했다.  주간으로 보면 S&P500은 0.5%, 나스닥은 0.7% 내려 두 주 연속 하락을 기록했고, 다우만 0.4% 올라 3주 연속 상승 흐름을 지켰다. 이 숫자 자체가 지금 시장의 성격을 말해준다. 돈이 시장을 빠져나가는 게 아니라 AI 성장주에서 빠져나와 경기방어와 배당 쪽으로 옮겨 다니고 있다는 뜻이다. 다만 금요일은 그 피난처마저 흔들렸다는 점에서 전날과 결이 달랐다.  장중 흐름  출발부터 좋지 않았다. 개장 직후 다우는 530포인트 이상 밀렸고, S&P500과 나스닥은 5주 만의 최저 수준까지 내려갔다. 전날 투매의 중심이었던 반도체와 빅테크에서 저가 매수가 유입되며 나스닥은 장중 플러스로 돌아섰고 한때 0.2% 상승하기도 했으나, 오후 들어 유가가 다시 밀어 올려지자 지수 전체가 힘을 잃었다. 나스닥은 결국 막판에 상승폭을 반납하고 소폭 하락으로 마쳤다.  시장 폭은 나빴다. S&P500 구성종목 중 네 종목 가운데 세 종목꼴로 하락했다. 전날은 AI 관련주가 폭락하는 와중에도 상승·하락 종목 수가 거의 1대1이었다는 점을 떠올리면, 금요일의 하락은 '좁고 깊은' 하락이 아니라 '넓고 얕은' 하락이었다. 공포지수 VIX는 2% 오른 19.5로 마감해 주간으로는 35%가량 치솟았는데, 이는 6월 초 이후 가장 큰 주간 상승폭이다.  유가, 4년여 만의 최고치로 다시 시장을 짓누르다  이날 시장을 지배한 변수는 AI가 아니라 원유였다. 브렌트유 12월물은 3.1% 오른 배럴당 116.7달러에 마감해 2022년 6월 이후 최고 수준을 찍었고, 3주 연속 주간 상승을 기록했다. WTI도 4% 가까이 뛰어 103달러 선을 넘어섰다. 10월 초만 해도 브렌트유는 97달러를 밑돌았으니, 한 달도 안 되는 사이에 20달러가 올라온 셈이다.  배경은 중동이다. 후티 반군의 사우디아라비아 에너지 시설 공격이 전해졌고, 홍해 인근 공격과 UAE 당국이 보고한 원유 유출 사고까지 겹치며 공급 차질 우려가 커졌다. 여기에 트럼프 대통령이 이틀 연속으로 중간선거 이후 이란 문제를 "끝장낼지, 아니면 그냥 말라죽게 둘지" 고민하고 있다는 식의 발언을 내놓으면서, 시장은 호르무즈 해협을 둘러싼 대치가 장기화될 가능성을 가격에 반영하기 시작했다. 유엔 주재 미국 대사가 전쟁이 1년 더 갈 수도 있다고 언급한 보도도 같은 방향으로 작용했다.  유가 급등의 직격탄은 항공주가 맞았다. 유나이티드, 델타, 아메리칸항공이 나란히 하락했고 운송 섹터 전반이 약세였다. 반면 S&P500 에너지 섹터 지수는 장중 사상 최고치를 경신했다. 지수가 빠지는 날 에너지가 신고가를 쓴다는 것은 이번 하락의 성격이 성장 둔화가 아니라 비용 압박, 즉 인플레이션 쪽에 가깝다는 신호다.  다우를 끌어내린 종목들  다우 하락폭이 유독 컸던 이유는 몇몇 대형 구성종목의 개별 악재가 유가 쇼크와 겹쳤기 때문이다. 가장 큰 짐은 아메리칸익스프레스였다. 3분기 매출이 전년 대비 9% 늘어난 145억 달러, 조정 주당순이익이 13% 늘어난 4.68달러로 이익은 시장 예상을 넘겼지만, 매출이 컨센서스였던 148억 달러에 미치지 못했다. 여기에 전 세계 인력의 약 5%, 3,500명가량을 감원하는 구조조정 계획과 3억 3,600만 달러의 구조조정 비용을 함께 발표하자 주가는 3.5~3.7% 밀렸다. CEO가 "AI에 대비하기 위해" 더 민첩하고 효율적인 조직이 필요하다고 설명한 대목은, 이달 초 자금세탁방지 통제 미비로 3억 5,000만 달러 벌금을 부과받은 직후라는 점에서 더 무겁게 받아들여졌다.  캐터필러가 2%가량 내렸고 골드만삭스도 1% 넘게 하락해 금융주 전반이 약세였다. 전날 AI 투매 속에서 피난처 역할을 했던 필수소비재, 유틸리티, 헬스케어 같은 방어 섹터마저 이날은 모두 하락했다. 금리가 다시 오르자 배당주의 상대 매력이 줄어든 탓이다.  통신주도 눈에 띄게 흔들렸다. 블룸버그가 스페이스X가 미국 전역 8만 개 통신 기지국 부지 임대를 두고 크라운캐슬, 아메리칸타워와 협상 중이라고 보도하자 AT&T, 버라이즌, T모바일이 장 초반부터 급락했다. 번스타인은 약 300억 달러의 주파수 투자에 이어 8만 개 기지국까지 확보한다면 이는 전국 단위 지상 무선망 구축에 필요한 규모이며 "돌이킬 수 없는 지점"이 될 수 있다고 평가했다.  AI 트레이드, 반등은 했지만 불안은 남았다  전날 급락의 진원지였던 AI 관련주는 금요일 혼조세로 숨을 골랐다. 마이크론이 2.5%, 인텔과 AMD가 각각 1.7%, 마이크로소프트가 0.7% 올라 지수 낙폭을 줄이는 데 기여했다. 엔비디아는 보합권에서 등락을 반복했다. 다만 코어위브 같은 네오클라우드 종목들은 자금조달 비용 상승과 설비투자 둔화 가능성이라는 전날의 걱정거리가 그대로 남아 반등이 약했다.  이번 조정의 발단을 다시 짚어보면, 목요일 젠슨 황이 네오클라우드 인프라 수요는 "차트를 뚫을 정도"지만 자본 부족이 성장을 막고 있다고 발언한 것이 시장을 자극했다. 수요가 아니라 돈이 문제라는 말은, 지금까지 AI 설비투자를 '얼마나 쓰느냐'로 평가하던 시장에 '어떻게 조달하느냐'라는 새로운 질문을 던졌다. 여기에 메타가 3분기 매출 호조에도 불구하고 설비투자 가이던스 하단을 1,300억 달러에서 1,350억 달러로 올리고, 클라우드 용량·전력 계약·하드웨어 관련 각종 지출 약정이 8,250억 달러에 달한다고 공개하면서 전날 7% 급락했었다. 메타가 AI 자금조달을 위해 무의결권 신주 발행을 발표한 것도 기존 주주 입장에서는 희석 우려로 읽혔다.  금요일 메타는 프리마켓부터 낙폭을 일부 만회했고, 테슬라는 0.6% 내린 372달러 선으로 비교적 안정됐다. 테슬라는 지난 실적 발표에서 설비투자 계획을 50억 달러 줄였는데, 모건스탠리조차 2040년까지 사이버캡 500만 대 규모를 가정하고 있다는 점에서 로보택시 장기 스토리에 대한 신뢰는 아직 크게 흔들리지 않았다는 평가다. JP모건은 스페이스X 경영진과의 대화에서 회사가 메타와 달리 증자를 검토하지 않고 있으며 부채 쪽에 여러 자금 조달 수단이 있다고 밝혔다고 전했다.  스페이스X는 1.9% 오른 147.5달러로 마감했다. 수요일 3분기 실적 호조와 머스크의 테슬라 합병 지지 발언으로 급등했던 것을 목요일에 전부 반납한 뒤, 금요일 기지국 임대 보도로 다시 반등한 모양새다. 3분기 스타링크 중심의 커넥티비티 매출은 69% 늘어난 52억 달러였고, 분기 중 가입자 160만 명이 늘어 총 1,400만 명에 육박했다.  보켓캐피털의 김 포레스트 CIO는 로이터에 지금의 매도세가 단기적으로 과도하며 펀더멘털상 이유를 찾기 어렵다면서, AI는 긴 사이클의 초입인데 시장이 그 사이클을 너무 짧게 봤던 것이 문제라고 말했다. 다른 쪽에서는 메타 실적 이후 AI 트레이드에 대한 불안이 여전하고, 중동 상황은 좋아지는 게 아니라 나빠지는 쪽이라는 지적도 나왔다.  사이버보안주만 역주행  이날 시장에서 가장 선명하게 빛난 곳은 사이버보안이었다. 세일포인트, 클라우드플레어, 팔로알토네트웍스가 나란히 7% 넘게 급등했다. 에버코어 ISI가 보안 예산 전망이 강화되고 있다는 채널 설문 결과를 내놓은 것이 계기였는데, 지출의 초점이 데이터·AI·신원·클라우드 보안에 맞춰져 있다는 내용이었다. 옥타와 포티넷도 파이프라인이 탄탄한 업체로 거론됐다. 퍼스트트러스트 사이버보안 ETF는 이달 초 사상 최고치를 찍은 데 이어 최근 5거래일간 약 7% 올랐다. AI 설비투자에는 물음표가 붙었지만, AI 에이전트가 강력해질수록 보안 지출은 늘어난다는 논리가 돈을 끌어모았다.  시가총액 1위 자리를 두고 벌어진 공방  애플이 이날 장중 엔비디아를 제치고 시가총액 1위에 올랐다가 다시 내줬다. 두 회사 모두 약 5조 1,000억 달러 수준으로 목요일 종가 기준 격차가 1% 미만이었던 터라, 1,999달러짜리 아이폰 듀오 출시일과 맞물린 애플의 사상 최고가 랠리가 순위를 잠시 뒤집었다. 애플이 엔비디아를 추월한 것은 이번이 다섯 번째인데 그동안 오래 유지된 적은 거의 없었다.  개별 종목 이슈  모더나는 개인 맞춤형 흑색종 백신 3상 데이터 유출 여파로 목요일 17% 넘게 폭락했던 충격에서 벗어나, 금요일 하락 출발 후 장중 플러스로 돌아서며 낙폭을 일부 만회했다. SK하이닉스는 낸드 자회사 솔리다임의 미국 상장 계획을 시장 상황과 주가 흐름을 이유로 보류한다고 밝혔다. 솔리다임은 최대 1,500억 달러 가치로 100억~150억 달러 조달을 노렸던 초대형 딜이었다. SK하이닉스 미국 주식은 7월 공모가 149달러를 아직 밑돌고 있고 9월 고점 대비로는 3분의 1가량 낮은 수준이어서, 올해 미국 상장 외국기업 최대 규모였던 자사 상장이 물밑에 있는 상황에서 자회사 상장을 밀어붙이기 어려웠던 것으로 보인다.  채권·금리·달러·원자재  목요일 기술주 투매 때 채권으로 자금이 몰리며 10년물 금리가 2년여 만에 가장 큰 하루 낙폭을 기록하고 5% 아래로 내려왔었는데, 금요일에는 유가 상승이 인플레이션 우려를 다시 자극하며 금리가 되올랐다. 10년물은 4.99%로 마감해 5% 선 바로 아래에서 버텼다. 금리가 5%에 재도전하는 모양새가 다시 만들어졌다는 점이 주식시장에는 부담이다.  연준은 다음 주 10월 28일 회의를 앞두고 있다. 유가발 인플레이션 때문에 한때 인상 가능성까지 거론됐지만, 연방기금 선물시장에 반영된 10월 인상 확률은 9월 말 37%, 이번 주 초 15%에서 금요일 5% 안팎까지 내려왔다. 시장은 동결을 거의 확정적으로 보고 있으며, 관심은 파월 의장이 유가와 고용 사이에서 어떤 톤을 택하느냐에 쏠려 있다.  금은 1.2% 내린 온스당 4,010달러로 밀렸고 비트코인은 0.5%가량 하락한 8만 800달러 선에서 거래됐다. 주식이 빠지는 날 금까지 함께 내린 것은 금리 반등의 영향으로 풀이된다.  정리하며  이번 주 미국 증시는 세 개의 질문을 동시에 받았다. AI 설비투자는 누가 어떤 돈으로 감당하는가, 중동발 유가는 어디까지 가는가, 그리고 금리는 5%를 다시 넘을 것인가. 목요일은 첫 번째 질문이, 금요일은 두 번째와 세 번째 질문이 시장을 움직였다. 지수 낙폭만 보면 금요일은 전날보다 완만했지만, 네 종목 중 세 종목이 빠지고 방어주마저 밀렸다는 점에서 체감 온도는 더 낮았다.  다음 주는 연준 회의와 함께 애플·마이크로소프트·알파벳·아마존 등 남은 빅테크 실적이 몰려 있는 주간이다. 메타가 던진 '설비투자와 자금조달' 프레임이 다른 하이퍼스케일러에게도 똑같이 적용될지, 아니면 메타 고유의 문제로 좁혀질지가 AI 트레이드의 단기 방향을 가를 것이다. 유가는 중간선거 이후 이란 정책 변화 가능성과 홍해·사우디 정세를 계속 가격에 반영할 가능성이 크며, 브렌트 116달러 위에서 머무는 동안에는 항공·운송·소비재의 마진 압박 논의가 이어질 것이다.  유의사항  이 글은 특정 종목이나 자산에 대한 매수·매도 추천이 아니며, 전날 미국 시장의 흐름을 정리한 정보 제공 목적의 글입니다. 투자에 대한 판단과 책임은 전적으로 투자자 본인에게 있습니다.

#wallstreet #리서치보고서 #Newyorktimes #언론 #시사 #외신 #시각화요약   참고만하세요!  2026년 10월 24일 오전 9시 46분 한국 시간, 뉴욕 현지 10월 23일 오후 8시 46분 기준으로 정리해 드리겠습니다. 현재 공개적으로 확인되는 최신 보도는 주로 뉴욕 현지 23일자 기사입니다. 원문 직접 열람이 제한되어 기사 제목과 공개 설명을 살펴보고, 주요 사실은 공식 자료와 독립 보도로 보완했습니다. 아래의 편집 방향과 전망은 확인한 자료를 연결한 제 해석입니다.  이번 보도에서 두드러지는 흐름은 중간선거를 앞둔 제도적 긴장, 전쟁이 키우는 경제적 부담, 기술 변화에 대응하려는 정부의 역할 확대입니다. 선거 보도는 표심과 의석 전망에서 결과 인증과 패배 수용의 문제로 넓어지고 있습니다. 우크라이나 지원 논란은 미국 상원의 인준 권한과 연결됐으며, AI와 반도체 보도에서는 정부가 노동자를 보호하고 산업에 직접 투자하는 방식이 함께 다뤄졌습니다. 여러 사안에서 정책의 목표뿐 아니라 권한과 비용, 책임을 어떻게 배분할지가 쟁점으로 떠올랐습니다.  미국 중간선거 보도에서는 먼저 선거 절차에 대한 신뢰와 정치세력의 결과 수용에 대한 신뢰를 구분할 필요가 있습니다. 뉴욕타임스·시에나 조사에 관한 공개 설명은 대다수 유권자가 선거가 정확하게 치러질 것으로 보면서도, 약 절반은 공화당이 결과를 뒤집으려 할 가능성을 우려한다고 전합니다. 두 태도는 서로 다른 질문에 대한 반응입니다. 투·개표가 제대로 이루어질 것이라는 기대와, 패배한 정치세력이 그 결과를 받아들일 것이라는 기대는 별개이기 때문입니다. 이번 보도는 선거의 신뢰가 집계의 정확성과 결과 수용이라는 두 조건에 달려 있음을 보여줍니다. 뉴욕타임스 여론조사 기사 공개 정보  이러한 긴장을 구체적으로 드러내는 사례가 알래스카 상원선거 결과 인증을 둘러싼 소송입니다. AP의 알래스카 소송 보도  이 사건의 의미는 선거 경쟁이 투표 이전의 설득에서 투표 이후의 인증과 해석으로까지 확대되고 있다는 데 있습니다. 향후 쟁점은 후보를 구분하는 투표용지의 표시, 실제 혼동을 보여주는 증거, 유권자의 의사를 사후에 판단하는 기준이 될 것으로 보입니다. 결과가 나오기 전에 적용 기준이 충분히 설명되고 일관되게 유지되는지도 중요합니다. 개별 후보의 이해관계와 전체 선거 절차의 신뢰가 충돌할 수 있는 만큼, 법원이 어떤 근거와 범위에서 판단하는지 살펴볼 필요가 있습니다.  표심을 얻기 위한 경쟁도 마지막까지 치열합니다. 뉴욕타임스의 공개 기사 소개에 따르면, 선거 마지막 2주 동안 약 14억 달러 규모의 정치광고가 방영될 예정입니다. 이는 이미 집행된 총액이 아니라 예정된 광고 규모입니다. 거액의 광고 예약은 양당이 설득과 투표 참여에 자원을 집중하고 있음을 보여주지만, 그 자체로 효과나 승리를 보장하지는 않습니다. 남은 기간의 핵심은 생활비와 정부의 책임, 후보자의 신뢰성에 관한 메시지가 유권자에게 얼마나 설득력 있게 받아들여지는지입니다. 뉴욕타임스 광고전 보도의 공개 정보  국제 분야에서는 우크라이나 위성통신 제한을 둘러싼 통신 제한의 기술적·계약상 책임도 아직 규명해야 할 사안입니다. 뉴욕타임스 관련 기사 공개 정보, 의원들의 공식 발표  여기서 새롭게 드러나는 방향성은 군사 지원의 신뢰성이 미국 국내의 권한 행사와 연결되고 있다는 것입니다. 의회는 지원의 지속성과 조건을 확인하기 위해 인준과 계약 감독이라는 수단을 활용하려 하고 있습니다. 우크라이나에 필요한 것은 지원 변화가 가격의 움직임과 함께 확인돼야 합니다.  중동 보도는 에너지시장과 함께 서안지구 민간인의 생계와 안전에도 주목했습니다. 뉴욕타임스는 올리브 수확기에 정착민들의 농민 공격과 주택 포위가 발생하며 두려움이 커진 상황을 다뤘습니다. 앞서 발표된 유엔 인도주의업무조정국 보고서도 수확 관련 공격과 인명·재산 피해를 기록했습니다. 올리브 수확은 지역의 문화적 관행인 동시에 가구의 소득과 연결된 활동입니다. 농지에 접근하지 못하거나 나무가 훼손되는 피해는 한 차례의 충돌 이후에도 다음 수확과 생활의 기반에 영향을 남길 수 있습니다. 뉴욕타임스의 올리브 수확기 보도, 유엔 OCHA 상황 보고서  이러한 기사는 분쟁을 군사적 충돌의 횟수와 규모로만 평가하기 어려운 이유를 보여줍니다. 민간인이 일하고 이동하며 재산을 지킬 수 있는지가 생활의 지속성을 결정하기 때문입니다. 앞으로 현지 상황을 판단할 때는 공격의 발생과 함께 농지 접근과 수확 활동이 보장되는지, 피해에 대한 조사와 보호 조치가 실제로 작동하는지도 살펴야 합니다. 보도의 관심이 폭력의 순간에서 그 이후의 생계와 공동체 유지로 이어지고 있다는 점이 중요하게 읽힙니다.  기술 분야에서는 AI로 인한 고용 변화에 대비해 실업보험과 전환기 소득 지원을 강화하려는 입법 논의가 부각됐습니다. 23일 공개된 상원 재무위원회 민주당 간사실 발표에 따르면, 론 와이든 의원 등이 제시한 초안은 실업보험의 최소 기준과 지원 범위를 강화하고, AI 변화로 일자리를 잃은 노동자가 교육과 재훈련을 받는 동안 소득 안정을 돕는 프로그램을 제안합니다. 현재는 입법 초안으로, 새 급여가 이미 시행되고 있는 단계는 아닙니다. 뉴욕타임스의 AI 고용 대응 기사, 상원 재무위원회 공식 발표  이번 제안은 AI가 전국적인 대량 실업을 이미 일으켰다는 확정적 진단보다, 변화가 현실화될 때 기존 안전망이 충분히 대응할 수 있는지를 미리 점검하려는 움직임으로 이해하는 것이 적절합니다. 관심도 일자리 수의 증감에서 재교육 기간의 생활비와 새로운 직업으로 이동하는 데 필요한 시간으로 넓어지고 있습니다. 데이터센터의 비용 분담에 관한 별도 세제 초안도 함께 제시됐다는 점에서, 기술 산업의 성장과 전환 비용을 어떻게 연결할지에 대한 논쟁이 구체화되고 있습니다. 향후에는 지원 대상과 재원, 입법 합의가 핵심 쟁점이 될 것으로 보입니다.  반도체 분야에서는 정부가 산업의 투자와 지분 구조에 직접 참여하는 방식이 조명됐습니다. 뉴욕타임스의 23일 기사는 앞서 14일 발표된 미일 반도체 투자 구상을 다룹니다. 공식 발표에 따르면 일본이 최대 210억 달러의 자금을 제공하고 글로벌파운드리스가 기술 제공과 운영을 맡는 신규 공장 계획입니다. 별도 합의로 미 상무부가 글로벌파운드리스 지분 약 4%를 받는다는 내용도 포함됐습니다. 공장에 관한 소유·운영 구조와 기업 자체의 지분은 구분해야 하며, 투자 발표가 곧 완공이나 생산 개시를 의미하는 것은 아닙니다. 뉴욕타임스의 미일 반도체 거래 기사, 글로벌파운드리스 공식 발표  이 사례는 정부의 산업정책이 규제와 보조금 지급에서 자본과 사업 성과에 대한 참여로 확대되는 모습을 보여줍니다. 공급망 안정과 국내 생산 확대라는 목표를 추진하는 동시에, 공적 자금과 민간 경영의 책임을 어떻게 나눌지가 중요해집니다. 향후 평가는 투자 규모의 발표에 머물기보다 실제 건설 일정과 생산 능력, 계약상 책임, 사업 성과가 확인되는 과정에서 이루어져야 하겠습니다. AI 노동지원 논의와 함께 보면 기술의 성장에 정부가 관여하는 방식이 산업 육성과 사회적 비용 분담의 양쪽에서 넓어지고 있습니다.  유럽에서는 프랑스가 새로운 시위에 대비해 치안 대응을 강화하는 상황이 다뤄졌습니다. AFP에 따르면 정부는 24일 시위를 앞두고 약 7만 명의 경찰과 헌병을 배치할 계획이라고 밝혔습니다. 교육환경에 대한 학생들의 요구에서 시작된 시위는 생활비 부담에 대한 불만과 결합해 확산됐으며, 정부는 폭력과 약탈을 막기 위한 대응을 강조하고 있습니다. 동시에 집회 제한을 둘러싼 비판도 제기됩니다. 질서와 안전을 확보하는 조치가 진행되는 가운데, 학생과 시민의 요구에 어떤 구체적인 답변이 제시되는지가 향후 갈등의 방향을 가를 것으로 보입니다. AFP의 프랑스 시위 대응 보도  이번 기사들에서 제가 읽은 뉴욕타임스의 편집 방향은 불안을 설명하는 데서 나아가, 그 불안을 다루는 권한과 비용이 누구에게 배분되는지를 점검하는 데 관심이 모여 있다는 것입니다. 선거에서는 결과를 인증하고 받아들이는 절차를, 우크라이나 지원에서는 필수 기술을 제공하는 조건과 의회의 감독을 살피고 있습니다. 에너지와 서안지구 보도는 전쟁의 시장 비용과 민간인의 생활 기반을 함께 다루며, 기술 보도는 성장의 이익과 전환의 부담을 누가 감당할지 묻고 있습니다. 이는 이번에 확인한 기사들의 공통 관심사에 대한 해석이며, 매체 전체의 공식 입장을 뜻하지는 않습니다.  향후에는 선거 관련 요구가 법원과 선거 관리 절차에서 어떻게 검증되는지, 우크라이나 통신 복구와 의회의 인준 압박이 실제로 어떤 결과를 낳는지 확인해야 합니다. 경제적으로는 유가 상승이 얼마나 지속되고 실물 비용에 반영되는지가 중요합니다. AI 노동지원과 반도체 투자에서는 초안과 발표가 구체적인 합의·집행으로 이어지는지가 관건입니다. 이러한 이행 결과를 함께 살펴보시면, 오늘의 긴장이 일시적인 정치적 충돌에 머무는지 더 오래가는 제도와 경제 구조의 변화로 이어지는지 보다 분명하게 판단하실 수 있을 것입니다.

sample_tweets.text: Source: thehackernews.com/2026/10/le…

Leaked LiteLLM master key sat unrevoked for months before an attacker used it to hijack the PyPI release pipeline and push a backdoored Python package that activates on Python startup, even without importing the library.  Key findings:  - The attack chain began May 27, 2026, when a config file containing the LiteLLM Agent Platform master key was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repo. The key was identified quickly and the commit force-pushed over, but revocation never happened. On October 10, an attacker operating from 69.48.229[.]143 used that still-valid key to authenticate to the Agent Platform and extract a GitHub CLI OAuth token tied to an org owner account, granting full write access across all repositories.  - The attacker then ran two short-lived malicious workflows via throwaway branches named ci-tmp-a351cc and ci-tmp-4d8517, each pushing .github/workflows/cache.yml with the benign-looking commit message "ci: bump cache config." The branches were created, triggered, and deleted within minutes. This is why the activity leaves almost no trace in ordinary repository history. Both workflows exfiltrated secrets to webhook[.]site/65a42464-3cfa-4b02-a18c-17a6d7b86f37 and webhook[.]site/4da03473-a3e7-4dc2-a087-9c564b4208e1. Harvested material included GitHub tokens, a GitHub App private key and signing key, Linear workspace session state, OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Tavily, Together AI, GitGuardian, PostgreSQL credentials, Redis credentials, and Playwright serialized browser storage state. The GitGuardian key is notable: it gave the attacker control over the secret-scanning platform that would otherwise surface this activity.  - On October 21, the attacker overrode branch protections and repointed the release pipeline source from BerriAI/litellm to the lookalike Berri-AI/litellm. Using one stolen engineer token to trigger and a second to approve, LiteLLM version 1.107.0 was published to PyPI at 11:39 a.m. UTC, with Docker Hub and GHCR images following at 11:46 a.m. Run records were deleted by 11:54 a.m. PyPI quarantined 1.107.0 at 1:23 p.m., about 77 minutes after a researcher reported the supply chain compromise.  - The malicious package installs components outside the LiteLLM application directory so they survive application removal and execute automatically at Python startup regardless of whether LiteLLM is imported. It runs two paths: a credential harvester targeting SSH files, Git and GitLab tokens, environment variables, npm, PyPI, pip, Yarn, Maven, Gradle, Composer, RubyGems, and Cargo tokens, plus cloud and browser credentials, exfiltrating compressed data via HTTP POST to litellm[.]dev/healthcheck (domain registered October 13, 2026). A second path launches a Unix backdoor as a background process that fetches and runs attacker-supplied code every hour.  DFIR takeaway: If LiteLLM 1.107.0 touched any environment, do not stop at removing the package. Inspect Python startup paths and site-packages directories outside the application install for malicious files dropped by the installer, because Microsoft's analysis confirms the startup components persist after the application is removed. Hunt outbound POST requests to litellm[.]dev/healthcheck and connections to webhook[.]site in network logs around October 10 and October 21. Audit GitHub Actions logs for workflow runs on branches matching ci-tmp- patterns that no longer exist, then cross-reference the repository activity log, which retains records even after branch deletion. Treat every secret that existed in the affected environment as compromised: rotate GitHub tokens, cloud API keys, database credentials, and any serialized session state. The IOCs and workflow analysis are in Socket's published report.  #DFIR_Radar

Exasol Database 7.1.30 ships a hardcoded SYS credential (sys / exasol) that grants full DBA access and OS command execution via a built-in Python UDF, scoring 8.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H).  - The credential pair sys / exasol is printed in the vendor's own docker-db README under "Connecting to the Database" and appears in two internal CI test scripts at /usr/opt/EXASuite-7/EXAClusterOS-7.1.30/docker/test/. Nothing in the container's init path rotates it, sets a must-change flag, or refuses service until it is changed. The ConfD AuthenticationToken and BucketFS WritePasswd are generated as per-deployment randoms; the most privileged credential is not. CWE-1392 is primary; CWE-94, CWE-798, CWE-78, CWE-1188, and CWE-250 are co-recorded.  - The two-step exploit chain requires no memory corruption or protocol bypass. Leg one: authenticate to the binary SQL service on port 8563 over TLS using the shipped constant. Leg two: issue four SQL statements (CREATE SCHEMA, OPEN SCHEMA, CREATE OR REPLACE PYTHON3 SCALAR SCRIPT with an os.popen body, SELECT) and read stdout back through the ordinary result set. No exfiltration channel is needed because the return value crosses the trust boundary in-band. The executing identity observed was uid=500(exadefusr) gid=500(exausers) groups=500(exausers),0(root); that supplementary root group under the vendor-required privileged container mode is a recognised escalation position, though escalation to uid=0 was not attempted or claimed.  - SYS authority over the SQL layer is the larger half of the impact: every schema, table, view, user, and privilege in the analytical warehouse is readable and writable without touching the script engine at all. An attacker can create additional accounts with chosen privileges, giving a durable second entry point that survives rotation of the factory credential. Availability follows the same authority. A separate smaller finding (not scored here): the BucketFS default bucket has Public=True, allowing unauthenticated read listing; write attempts returned 403 because the bucket WritePasswd is a per-deployment random.  - Detection is weak by design. Every step is legitimate product activity: a TLS handshake, a SYS login, a CREATE SCRIPT, and a SELECT. No [28000] authentication-failed sequence will precede a successful hit with the shipped constant. The highest-value detection signal is script-object creation logged with the creating user and source address; the report notes the default deployment does not surface this. A SYS session originating from an unexpected address is the next-best indicator, but operators who never rotated the credential have no baseline to compare against.  - The docker-db 7 deployment form is end-of-life on CentOS 7 and the vendor states no fix is planned for it. The CVE is pending. A conditional 9.8 Critical reading (AV:N) applies to multi-node --network=host deployments and any deployment where port 8563 is published without a loopback restriction. The full proof-of-concept (Python 3, standard library only, --allow-remote gated) and IOCs are in the report at 0day-rubbish[.]com/blog/exasol-database-default-credential-python-udf-os-popen-rce.  Hunt: enumerate all SCRIPT objects in Exasol system tables (EXA_ALL_SCRIPTS) for PYTHON3 bodies referencing os.popen, os.system, or subprocess. Cross-reference script creation timestamps against known administrator sessions. Rotate the SYS credential immediately; with the factory credential changed and no non-admin account holding script-creation rights, the report states this finding does not arise.  #DFIR_Radar

Beyond the public statistics we see coming out, what does AI use actually look like inside a large c

sample_tweets.text: SEX MAKES BILLIONS. WHO PAYS FOR THE RISK?  OnlyFans grew. Its subscription revenue fell. Its net profit barely moved.  Europe's STI numbers increased in some countries and fell in others. A promising prevention investment then met disappointing randomised-trial evidence.  These are connected stories about money, measurement and risk. They deserve a closer reading than either a moral panic or a celebration of platform growth.  I started with two articles in The Economist: “The new economics of sex work” and “Sexually transmitted infections are surging in Europe”. Then I went to company accounts, national statistics and original research. The four attached charts show the financial model, the country differences, the medical burden and the uncertainty around prevention. [1, 2]  Digital adult content, dating services, consensual paid sex and the population's wider sexual lives are distinct activities. Watching content does not transmit an infection. These data do not show that a platform caused an epidemic. The connection is the allocation of income, bargaining power, information and health risk.  Start with the money that can actually be audited. Fenix International, the company behind OnlyFans, reported $7.843 billion in gross site volume for its financial year ending in November 2025. Its own revenue was $1.553 billion. Profit before tax was $714.9 million. These are three different quantities: transactions through the platform, the revenue recognised by the intermediary and the profit remaining after its expenses. Calling the first figure “OnlyFans revenue” overstates the company's accounting revenue approximately fivefold. [3]  The distinction changes the interpretation of profitability. Pre-tax profit was 46.0% of platform revenue, but 9.1% of gross site volume. The difference between those percentages is the economic territory occupied by creators and the platform's accounting boundary. A high margin on the intermediary's recognised revenue says something about the profitability of intermediation; it does not establish that the entire production chain enjoys that margin.  The more revealing development is below the headline. Subscription revenue fell from $470.4 million in 2024 to $422.5 million in 2025, a decline of 10.2%. Non-subscription revenue rose from $942.7 million to $1.131 billion, an increase of 20.0%. That category, which includes one-off transactions such as messaging and access to content, supplied 72.8% of revenue in 2025. The combined business grew while its subscription component contracted.  There is a second complication. Revenue rose 9.9%, but net profit increased only 0.2%, to $521.4 million. Administrative expenses rose 24.4%; the pre-tax margin fell from 48.4% to 46.0%, and the tax charge increased. The company remained highly profitable and paid $535 million in dividends during the year. Yet the direction of earnings is more nuanced than the direction of sales. Rapid monetisation does not automatically produce equally rapid growth in distributable economic value.  Fenix also reported 5.063 million creator accounts and 437.133 million fan accounts. Its definition covers accounts created and not subsequently deleted or deactivated. These are not counts of full-time workers or paying subscribers. Dividing aggregate creator proceeds by the account stock would tell us little about median earnings, hours worked, taxes or costs. The income distribution matters more than a misleading average.  This is a platform problem with highly personal stakes. Creators supply much of the production effort, promotion and reputational exposure; the intermediary supplies infrastructure, distribution, payment processing and rules. An individual can leave with skills and perhaps an audience, but cannot necessarily take the platform's discovery system or payment relationships along. The relevant labour question is the strength of that person's outside option. Revenue participation can coexist with weak bargaining power, especially when the income distribution and the cost of acquiring customers remain opaque.  Geography adds another layer. The Fenix accounts disclose $965.4 million of revenue from the United States, $346.8 million from the UK and Europe combined, and $241.1 million from the rest of the world. The US therefore contributed 62.2% of recognised revenue. The European category grew 22.2%, faster than the total. But the accounts do not split that category into France, Italy, Germany or other individual markets. Country rankings inferred from website traffic would introduce assumptions about spending per visitor that the accounts do not verify.  Grindr, an adjacent dating and social platform, reported $439.9m in 2025 revenue, $195.6m in adjusted EBITDA and $94.8m in net income. A 44.5% adjusted EBITDA margin and a 21.5% net margin describe different things. The adjustments include $54.5m of stock-based compensation. Valuation requires attention to the exclusions, not simply the larger number. [4]  Italy offers a different accounting lens. Istat estimated household consumption of prostitution services at €5.0bn in 2024 and associated value added at €4.2bn, both up 2.8% on its unrounded estimates. These are modelled national-account quantities, not audited company sales or profits. Value added is calculated after intermediate inputs; it cannot be added to consumption as another market. Inclusion in GDP also says little about welfare, working conditions or the distribution of earnings. [5]  The country evidence makes that question harder, and more interesting, than a single European epidemic headline suggests. ECDC recorded 106,331 gonorrhoea notifications and 45,577 syphilis notifications for 2024. The headline gonorrhoea notification rate was 26.9 per 100,000 population. These are reported diagnoses under participating surveillance systems. Detection depends on access, testing intensity, the people tested, laboratory practice and reporting completeness as well as underlying transmission. [6, 7]  Spain reported 37,169 gonorrhoea cases and 11,556 syphilis cases in 2024, corresponding to notification rates of 76.4 and 23.8 per 100,000. Both counts increased from 2023. Portugal's gonorrhoea count was almost unchanged, at 2,764, while syphilis rose from 1,894 to 2,198. Even neighbouring countries therefore require different diagnostic questions. The composition of the increase matters for testing, partner services, clinical capacity and expenditure.  Ireland had the highest reported national gonorrhoea rate in the ECDC table, at 109.0 per 100,000. Yet its case count fell 11.6%, from 6,598 to 5,832. Denmark also recorded a decline. A high level and an improving annual trend can coexist. A minister rewarded solely for moving down a country ranking could misunderstand both the country's baseline and the role of its detection system.  Finland's gonorrhoea notifications rose 39.9%, from 1,329 to 1,859, while syphilis fell 33.0%, from 461 to 309. Sweden also combined a gonorrhoea increase with a syphilis decline. A composite STI growth rate would hide which infection needs more attention. Different infections create different demands on prevention, diagnosis and clinical capacity.  Italy's ECDC notifications increased from 2,355 to 3,105 for gonorrhoea, up 31.8%, and from 2,540 to 3,088 for syphilis, up 21.6%. Hungary's syphilis count rose 42.8%, to 1,725. Malta's rose from 124 to 340, a 174.2% increase. Malta's 60.3 per 100,000 rate deserves attention, but its small population also makes percentage movements more sensitive to comparatively small changes in case numbers. These are signals to investigate local transmission and detection, not a league table of sexual behaviour.  France, Belgium and the Netherlands create a different problem. Their ECDC figures come from sentinel surveillance, and the tables do not provide comparable national notification rates. Germany reported syphilis but no gonorrhoea data to this ECDC collection; Austria supplied neither in these tables. A blank cell represents an information gap. It cannot be converted into zero disease or evidence that a country is safer. The chart accompanying this article preserves those gaps rather than estimating them away.  England's newer data complicate the story further. In 2025, gonorrhoea diagnoses fell from 71,766 to 63,943, down 10.9%, and infectious syphilis diagnoses fell from 9,553 to 8,262, down 13.5%. Recorded sexual-health screens were almost unchanged. However, infectious syphilis among women who have sex with men rose from 838 to 878. The overall improvement therefore coexisted with deterioration in a subgroup relevant to pregnancy and congenital infection. England is also a distinct reporting geography and this is a later year than the EU/EEA comparison. [8]  In the Netherlands, sexual-health centres changed routine chlamydia testing in January 2025, generally restricting it to people with symptoms or a partner with relevant symptoms. RIVM explicitly warns that subsequent chlamydia diagnosis totals are not directly comparable with previous years. Meanwhile, gonorrhoea diagnoses at those centres rose from 13,952 to 14,297. A reduction in diagnoses following a change in whom a service tests cannot automatically be booked as prevention success. [9]  The United States provides a similar warning about aggregates. Provisional CDC data for 2024 showed more than 2.2 million reported cases across chlamydia, gonorrhoea and syphilis, with the combined count down 9%. Congenital syphilis nevertheless increased again, to nearly 4,000 cases. The system can improve on a large aggregate while failing on an outcome with particularly serious lifelong consequences. An economic assessment must weight severity and distribution, not simply count events. [10]  How large is the financial burden? A widely used CDC-authored study estimated that eight STIs acquired in the United States in 2018 generated $15.9 billion in discounted lifetime direct medical costs, expressed in 2019 dollars. The study included sexually acquired HIV, which accounted for $13.7 billion, or approximately 86% of the total. It excluded prevention expenditure, lost productivity and costs associated with maternal transmission, such as congenital syphilis. [11]  The date and accounting basis belong in the headline. This is the present value of future medical costs arising from one year's infections. It is not a measured annual bill for 2026, not a global estimate and not the cost of the three bacterial infections alone. Putting it next to an annual platform revenue figure may illustrate scale, but dividing the two would not establish a subsidy or the share of harm caused by that platform. The populations, periods and causal boundaries differ.  The same study reveals a distributional imbalance. Excluding HIV, women bore approximately three-quarters of the estimated direct medical cost. Expected lifetime cost per infection was $262 for chlamydia in women versus $46 in men, and $254 versus $78 for gonorrhoea. Those averages reflect probabilities of treatment and complications; they are not the bill charged for every diagnosis. The implication is that the person represented most prominently in notification statistics need not be the person bearing the largest downstream cost per infection.  Medical claims also miss pain, infertility, lost working time, unpaid care and the consequences of stigma. Some of these losses can be valued through earnings or expenditure; others require measures of health and quality of life. Adding every valuation together without checking overlap would manufacture a false total. Exclusion from a medical-cost study does not make a loss economically irrelevant.  Time is another source of distortion. The US cost study used a 3% annual discount rate. Its underlying estimate for the lifetime medical cost of an HIV infection was $420,285 on that discounted basis, compared with approximately $1.08 million without discounting. The difference comes from when expenditures occur. A clinic is funded now; some benefits of preventing infection emerge decades later and may accrue to another insurer or public budget. The institution paying for prevention may capture only a fraction of the benefit it creates.  The institution funding prevention now may receive only part of the saving, years later. Annual budget control can favour postponing an expense even when postponement increases expected social costs. Cost-effective, cost-saving and profitable for a provider describe different tests. A credible investment case must identify the payer, beneficiary, time horizon and health outcome.  ECDC's policy monitoring exposes how basic some of the missing infrastructure remains. Among 29 reporting countries, 18 had a national STI strategy or policy, 13 reported out-of-pocket costs for basic tests, and only four submitted data on the proportion of pregnant women screened for syphilis. That last figure measures an information gap, not proof that the other countries fail to screen pregnant women. But a policy whose coverage cannot be measured is difficult to manage or evaluate. [12]  For a person facing a fee, travel time, lost earnings or fear of disclosure, testing has a price even when the laboratory procedure is inexpensive. Economic theory predicts that increasing the private cost can deter use. Because diagnosis and treatment can also benefit future partners, the social return to access may exceed the private return perceived by the person paying. The case for reducing barriers rests on that mechanism and should be tested against local service data, rather than assumed to produce the same return everywhere.  The Economist also points to uncomfortable evidence about regulation. Returning to the original research makes the scale clearer. Cunningham and Shah's study of the unexpected decriminalisation of indoor prostitution in Rhode Island found an expansion of the market alongside an approximately 30% reduction in reported rape offences and a reduction of more than 40% in female gonorrhoea incidence. This is a specific quasi-experimental result; it does not establish that every legal reform would have the same effects in every country. [1, 13]  Research by Cameron, Seager and Shah in East Java, Indonesia, examined an unexpected local criminalisation of sex work. Biologically measured STIs among female sex workers increased 58%, with reduced condom access and use identified as the mechanism. The researchers also found economic harm among women leaving the sector and pressure on their children's schooling. These results make it difficult to evaluate enforcement exclusively through arrests, closures or the visible size of a market. [14]  Technology offers another route into prevention. Grindr reports that the Together TakeMeHome programme has distributed more than one million free HIV self-test kits, with nearly half ordered directly through its app. This is a company-reported distribution measure, not an independently established estimate of infections prevented. It nevertheless illustrates how the same infrastructure used to reach customers can help reach people underserved by conventional health services. [15]  Prevention investment also needs protection from its own attractive narratives. When England began its targeted gonorrhoea vaccination programme in August 2025 using the meningococcal B vaccine 4CMenB, the government cited modelling suggesting up to 100,000 infections and more than £7.9 million in costs could be avoided over ten years. Those were projected outcomes conditional on assumptions about protection, uptake and transmission. They were never realised savings waiting in a bank account. [16]  In July 2026, the Australian GoGoVax randomised trial reported a materially different signal. Among 587 participants in the primary analysis, gonorrhoea incidence was 48.1 events per 100 person-years in the vaccine group and 47.8 in the placebo group. The incidence-rate ratio was 1.01, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.80–1.26. The trial did not demonstrate protection against gonorrhoea in the high-risk population studied. This finding concerns that use and population, not the vaccine's established meningococcal indication. [17]  An October 2026 meta-analysis of four randomised trials, conducted in France, Hong Kong and Australia and including 1,397 men who have sex with men, estimated a pooled incidence-rate ratio of 0.88, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.74–1.05. The interval includes no effect. It also leaves uncertainty about a possible benefit; it does not prove that protection is exactly zero in every population. The distinction between observational findings, trial populations and generalisation is central to the investment decision. [18]  The financial response is to update expected returns, test projections against efficacy uncertainty and reassess implementation as evidence develops. Retaining an optimistic savings forecast unchanged would be unsound. So would treating one disappointing strategy as evidence against prevention generally. Forecasts need a process for revision.  Antimicrobial resistance creates a different kind of investment problem. ECDC's July 2026 assessment described increases in ceftriaxone-resistant gonorrhoea and evidence of local transmission in several European countries. It judged the risk to the general population low at that time and reported that the documented cases had been successfully treated. The concern is the narrowing of effective treatment options and the possibility of more difficult management, rather than a claim that all gonorrhoea has already become untreatable. [19]  A financially serious response would put notifications beside testing volumes, positivity, population coverage and changes in definitions. It would connect prevention spending to completed care, time to treatment, reinfection and congenital outcomes. It would distinguish the next two years' budget impact from the value of a lifetime of better health.  Country-specific monetary estimates require another discipline. Multiplying Spain's reported gonorrhoea diagnoses by the American cost per infection would combine notifications with a model of all incident infections, different care prices, different treatment probabilities and a different population mix. It would yield a precise-looking answer to a poorly specified question. A defensible Spanish, Italian or Hungarian estimate would need local incidence assumptions, treatment pathways, complication risks and unit costs. Where those inputs are absent, publishing a national disease count is more informative than presenting an invented national financial liability.  Consider a deliberately narrow historical benchmark. At the US study's discounted estimate of $420,285 per HIV infection, $1 million in additional prevention spending would need to avert approximately 2.4 infections to offset that amount in direct lifetime medical costs alone. The calculation is arithmetic, not an evaluated programme: it uses 2019 US prices, assumes the full medical saving accrues to the decision-maker and says nothing about the achievable number of infections prevented. Real investment decisions require those missing inputs. Its value is to show why small absolute changes in a high-cost outcome can matter financially, while a large number of low-cost contacts may create little measurable return.  For private investors, durable cash flow depends on more than traffic and today's margins. Revenue concentration, creator retention, payment infrastructure, privacy and compliance costs all matter. Fenix's changing revenue mix and slower profit growth show why capitalising today's margin indefinitely is a demanding assumption. For governments, the corresponding discipline is to measure access, coverage and outcomes, and to identify which budget receives the benefit.  Sex is economically consequential because it combines valuable services, human agency, unequal bargaining positions and risks that travel beyond the original transaction. The aim should be to make the gains more durable and the costs more visible. We already know how to count a payment. The harder and more valuable task is to account for the person, the future and the institutions left carrying the risk.  Research cut-off: 24 October 2026. Beyond the public statistics we see coming out, what does AI use actually look like inside a large cybersecurity company? Here’s what I’m seeing at the company I work for. Is it being used? Well, yes, quite a bit, and adoption is spreading. The interesting part, though, is what people are doing with it.  First, what’s available today? In our case, we have access to various models (frontier or open-weight: OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, and we’re starting to see DeepSeek). We can use these models either directly or via API through an LLM proxy. Metrics are being introduced to give users more visibility into the cost of certain models and their suitability for a given task. The AI teams are also putting together a tool where you describe a need and get a recommendation for the most suitable model, both technically and economically. On the pentesting side, open-weight models are used much more than they are by the average user: Kimi, DeepSeek and others. We also have access to frontier models for offensive security use cases.  What are the use cases, and how far do they go? The two things I’m most interested in are the growth in usage and how useful that usage actually is. When it comes to adoption, what works best isn’t so much corporate communication campaigns as word of mouth. For someone unfamiliar with the subject, hearing about productivity gains through agents in an official announcement is pretty abstract… It means a lot more when a colleague tells you they’re automating their meeting notes from a Teams transcript, having AI create their PowerPoint presentations (steering committees/progress reviews/bids…), automating the drafting of technical deliverables from a report template, or scripting configuration migrations from vendor A to vendor B. That gets people curious and gives them a concrete idea of the time they could save. In just a few months, we’ve gone from simple writing/PowerPoint automation tools to building applications addressing a wider range of needs. Then, through those early adopters sharing their experiences, curiosity about “how it works” starts growing. People who were previously fairly “old school” or unfamiliar with all this start looking into how agents work, how to set them up and how to optimise them. A whole workplace ecosystem takes shape, with people talking, starting projects together, all with one single goal, and I’ll put it bluntly: making their lives less of a pain by spending less time doing boring, time-consuming crap.  Over the past few months, I’ve been seeing real momentum building around the creation of all sorts of tools to meet different needs specific to my sector: - Various automation scripts/apps (particularly for configuring/hardening systems) - Intelligent apps for incident aggregation/management (assigning incidents to analysts, behavioural analysis leading to suggested workflows…) - Tools for offensive and defensive security - Tools for cloud deployment - Automated reporting and project tracking, with efforts to connect them to operational tools and build an ecosystem - Plenty of others, as I can’t list every initiative underway across the different business units  In the detection and incident response business unit, some of these tools are already at the PoC stage.  The thing to take away is that these initiatives come from every level, from management to operational teams. That said, not everything is at the same stage: some things are being developed, some are being tested, and some are already used day to day. And behind all that, it takes time to test these tools, maintain them and adapt them to colleagues’ needs. Building something that works for yourself is one thing; getting a team to use it over time is another. Productivity gains still need to be assessed case by case, accounting for the checking required.  Senior management is giving these initiatives the green light, freeing up more and more funding (to pay for token usage!) to help them grow. The economics are becoming a real issue, though: while budgets are increasing, their allocation is now more tightly controlled (outlining the needs, writing specifications with expected productivity gains, potential for use across teams…).  We’re also seeing guardrails emerge around sovereignty, confidentiality and security, depending on the needs, particularly through the security department: where is the infrastructure hosted, which model is being used, what are the limits on data exposure, where should the tool be hosted if it gets built? A whole bunch of questions, addressed through forms to at least identify the use cases and what’s at stake.  That’s what I’m seeing today “on the ground” at a large cybersecurity company. What are you seeing in your own organisation?

The next morning, I emailed HR.  I attached the policy and asked why I had received a formal warning for leaving to collect my sick daughter when the company specifically allowed employees to request emergency time off for dependent care.  HR replied two days later.  They said the policy applied only when employees followed the proper notification process.  I sent them my email to my manager from the day of the incident.  It clearly stated that my daughter's school had called, that I needed to leave, and that I would finish my report from home.  My manager had replied:  “We'll discuss this on Monday.”  That was the only response I'd received before leaving.  A week later, HR scheduled another meeting.  This time, a senior HR manager attended.  She reviewed the emails and asked my manager whether he'd informed me about the emergency leave policy.  He said he hadn't thought it applied.  She asked why.  He said:  “Because the employee could have arranged alternative childcare.”  I explained that my wife was out of town and the school needed someone to collect our daughter immediately.  The HR manager looked at him and said:  “That isn't a reasonable expectation during an unexpected emergency.”  My written warning was withdrawn.  I thought that would be the end of it.  But two days later, my manager called me into his office.  He said he was disappointed that I'd escalated the matter.  Then he added:  “You've damaged the trust between us.”  I asked him whether he'd expected me to accept a disciplinary warning that shouldn't have been issued.  He said:  “Sometimes you have to decide whether being right is worth damaging your career.”  I didn't respond.  I documented the conversation and sent myself a dated note of what had been said.  Now things at work feel different.  I'm no longer invited to some meetings I used to attend.  My manager has started reviewing my work more closely than before.  I haven't been dismissed or formally disciplined again, but I'm beginning to wonder whether defending myself has made me a target.  Some colleagues say I should start looking for another job.  Others think I should make another formal complaint before things get worse.  My wife says I did the right thing because our daughter needed me.  I agree.  But I also know how difficult it can be to challenge someone who has influence over your career.  If your employer punished you for responding to a family emergency, would you challenge the decision even if it risked your career?  And if your manager started treating you differently afterward, would you report it or quietly find another job?

🚨 Who patrols Britain’s high streets, and who do they answer to?  The question is usually asked about the self-appointed anti-migrant “patrols” that have appeared in some towns, their members often dressed in black and masked by balaclavas, with no public mandate and no meaningful oversight. This piece is about something quieter and more official: a Reform-led council paying a private firm to patrol public space in response to concerns about asylum seekers.  For almost two centuries the main answer has been the police, a public service answerable, through law and elected oversight, to the public. In Essex, that answer is being rewritten. Since 14 September, private security guards hired by Reform-run Essex County Council have patrolled Braintree, Chelmsford and Colchester under the name Operation Vanguard (no relation to Merseyside Police’s operation of the same name). On a visit to Chelmsford on 15 October, Nigel Farage told the BBC he wanted the scheme “rolled out much more widely”.  Farage presents this as a rescue. The police, he claims, “do not fulfil the job, sadly, that they used to”, and Reform councils are right to start “filling that gap”. He has distanced himself from the masked groups: after the masked protests in Dover and Portsmouth in September, he said “Turning up in balaclavas is not the way to do it.” Vanguard is the version he does endorse. His claim about the police deserves testing against the evidence. It is also a policy proposal, and Essex is showing us what it looks like in practice.  The patrols are run by My Local Bobby, a private security firm founded in 2016 by former Metropolitan Police officers. It sells subscription “beats”, foot patrols paid for by residents or business districts, largely in affluent parts of London, and its guards are known as “Bobbies”. Its founder and chief executive, David McKelvey, a former Metropolitan Police detective chief inspector, is also chief operating officer of TM Eye, a linked firm that describes itself as the UK’s “leading private prosecutor”.  My Local Bobby’s latest accounts show its average number of employees rising from 80 to 140 in the year to November 2025. It is a growing business in a growing market. As a small company, it publishes no profit and loss account, so whether Vanguard makes it money cannot be seen from its public filings.  I first wrote about My Local Bobby in May 2018, when it announced plans to go nationwide after patrolling Belgravia, Mayfair and Kensington for subscribers paying up to £200 a month. McKelvey said then that the firm was taking things back to “Dixon of Dock Green-style policing”. I argued at the time that it amounted to a private police force for the “deserving” rich, while the “undeserving” poor could look out for themselves.  Eight years on, the model has changed shape. In Essex, the buyer is a council, the money is public, and the patrols were introduced in response to concerns about asylum seekers.  Essex gave it the Vanguard contract without competition. The official procurement notice records it as a “below threshold - without competition” award, worth £141,523.20 including VAT, and the council says a cabinet member decision “provided a waiver to enable a direct award”: its usual rules were set aside to hand the contract straight to one firm. It was signed on 11 September, three days before patrols began. There is no suggestion this was unlawful. But it meant a private firm was patrolling three town centres within months of Reform taking control of the county, with no competing bids.  The contract says the guards are there partly to “collect evidence if any incident occurs”, yet the only published report of their work records no figure for detentions and nothing on Wethersfield residents. Colchester’s crime and disorder committee has since asked how the firm was procured, and called for the local Community Safety Partnership to be properly involved before any extension.  Farage’s case rests on his claim that the police have “given up” on catching shoplifters. The BBC reported that Essex Police officers had secured more than 4,000 shop theft charges over the past year. In September, the force told Byline Times that all three centres “are safe places” with less crime than three years ago, and pointedly added that the most effective approach was a “joined-up” one with partners. The gap Vanguard was bought to fill was, by the council’s own launch report, one of feeling: the question, it said, was “not whether individual people represent a risk” but whether residents feared crime.  The national picture does not match Reform’s “Britain is broken” framing either. The Office for National Statistics bulletin published on 22 October found no statistically significant change in overall crime measured by the Crime Survey for England and Wales over the past year, and put it 14% lower than in 2017. Violence is 79% below its 1995 peak, and theft 77% below. Police recorded homicides, knife crime and firearms offences all fell in the year to June 2026, and recorded shoplifting fell 2% after a period of increases. Not everything is improving: fraud rose 11%, and the share of people who said they had experienced or witnessed antisocial behaviour rose from 36.7% to 41.4%. The ONS thinks most of that rise is genuine, though a change in how the question was asked inflated it.  Concern about antisocial behaviour is real. But it does not follow that the police have “given up”, still less that private patrols are the answer. Politicians who tell people Britain is broken, and certain news media that amplify that framing, help create the very fear that private patrols are then sold to soothe.  Then there is the distance between what residents were promised and what they got. The council’s guidance told the public the guards would have “no enforcement powers and no ability to arrest people”, and that they “cannot act on crimes themselves”. That wording was misleading. The guards have no special power of arrest, but like any member of the public they can make an arrest in the limited circumstances the law allows.  Just three days into the trial, two of them did exactly that, detaining two teenage girls suspected of shoplifting in Colchester and handcuffing them. Essex Police recorded two offences of assault without injury against the guards, raised concerns with the firm, and passed “learning” to it. The firm’s chief executive says his staff will keep detaining suspected offenders where justified. Across all the company’s beats, not Vanguard alone, he says they detain between 10 and 40 people a day, a figure that cannot be independently checked.  This is where privatisation stops being an abstraction. When a police officer handcuffs a teenager, a framework of accountability follows: codes of practice under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act, a statutory complaints system with independent oversight by the Independent Office for Police Conduct, misconduct procedures, a chief constable, and democratic oversight of the force by an elected police and crime commissioner. A private guard is subject to the criminal law, like anyone else, and needs a licence from the Security Industry Authority. But he is not subject to the statutory complaints and misconduct framework that governs police officers, and much of the day-to-day responsibility for supervising and disciplining him rests with his employer.  In Colchester, after police recorded two assaults, the Daily Gazette reports that the cases were closed under what Home Office counting rules call Outcome 20: “further action resulting from the crime report will be undertaken by another body or agency other than the police”. In practice, the “learning” went back to the firm. The council’s only published evaluation of Vanguard is a one-page report produced by that same firm and published by the council. It records activity: hours patrolled, reports filed and meetings attended. On the evidence published, it does not show whether crime fell or whether anyone feels safer.  These concerns are not confined to the scheme’s political opponents. When private patrols began spreading in Essex a decade ago, the county’s then police and crime commissioner, Nick Alston, warned they had “the potential to create a two-tier policing system”. The Police Federation has described private patrols as a “slow creep” towards exactly that, in which those who can pay get protection others cannot. The chairman of the Metropolitan Police Federation, while saying he would welcome extra patrols, was blunt about My Local Bobby’s staff: “They are NOT police officers and please do not ever kid yourself that they are.”  In 2019 the National Police Chiefs’ Council’s lead for local policing, Simon Cole, said such firms “should not replace or supplement policing”, and that intervening when a crime is committed is a job for properly trained officers. The police complaints watchdog has previously asked for powers to investigate private contractors carrying out police work. That proposal concerned contractors given police powers. Vanguard’s guards have none.  Criminologists have studied this for three decades. In 1996, David Bayley and Clifford Shearing described policing being “pluralised”, as private security moved into work once assumed to belong to the state. Ian Loader asked how plural policing could be governed democratically. Adam Crawford and Stuart Lister, studying private residential patrols, found that such patrols struggled to build the local knowledge and relationships that make policing work, and that the question of who oversees them remained unresolved.  One 2004 study of a British community with a commercial patrol, known in the literature as Merryville, found residents giving tacit support to guards targeting particular groups they saw as threats to their “mental comfort”. Set that beside a scheme whose founding report made fear of crime the test, and which the Daily Mail described as guards “hired to monitor asylum seekers”. The council says its guards would not know whether someone was an asylum seeker unless it was “self-declared or self-evident from the circumstances”. What circumstances? Asylum status cannot be seen. The wording leaves open who might be treated as suspicious, and on what basis.  Vanguard also matters because of where Reform wants to go nationally. The party has promised a “vast expansion” of stop and search, including “saturation policing”. It has promised a UK Deportation Command to “track down, detain and deport” people in the country illegally, which Reuters described as similar to America’s ICE. Reform’s home affairs spokesman, Zia Yusuf, insists it would not be the same, and says its officers would not be expected to carry weapons.   Vanguard is nothing like that agency: its guards have no immigration powers, and a council has no role in immigration enforcement. But it does establish a model: uniformed patrols in public space, delivered by a private contractor, introduced in response to concerns about asylum seekers, and supervised largely by their employer. Whether or not Essex is testing the water, it is showing what the water feels like.  None of this is new. Before 1829, London’s patchwork of policing included private thief-takers, paid by results and answerable to almost no one; the most notorious, Jonathan Wild, ran the thieves as well as catching them. The Metropolitan Police were created partly to end that arrangement, on the principle, attributed to Sir Robert Peel, that “the police are the public and the public are the police”. A public body, accountable to the public, patrolling public space.  The pressures on neighbourhood policing are real, and people are right to want visible patrols. But there are accountable ways to provide them. Colchester already employs neighbourhood wardens. One of its cabinet members, Martin Goss, said £50,000 could have funded a full-time council warden, with greater legal powers than Vanguard’s guards, for a year. This BRICS News post, amplified by Rep. Mike Rulli, is based on a real incident, but it’s packaged in a way that misleads.  The arrest did happen. On 3 August, four West Midlands Police officers arrested Fraser, a 15-year-old Reform activist from Walsall, at his home after a series of Facebook posts about Simon Bennett, Conservative group leader on Wolverhampton City Council. According to the Telegraph, he was fingerprinted and photographed, and his DNA was taken. That is routine for anyone arrested for a recordable offence in England and Wales, children included.  The arrest itself is where the real argument lies. If he is never charged, his DNA profile should normally be deleted.  First problem: “JUST IN”. The arrest took place almost twelve weeks ago, and national coverage began in early October after the Telegraph ran the story. It had already been circulating for more than a fortnight when BRICS News presented it as breaking news.  Polymarket pushed out a near-identical “JUST IN” post, adding that his devices were seized (see below).  Second problem: the rabbit picture. It was one post among several, and the least serious of them.   According to the Telegraph, the posts criticised Bennett for looking at his phone during a meeting and for turning up to a committee meeting in red shorts, a blue T-shirt and trainers. When he later wore a suit, Fraser thanked him for “not looking like rent boy”. An email from police to his lawyer reportedly said the comments could be considered a hate crime offence, and Bennett has described the “rent boy” remark as homophobic.  Bennett says the number of posts in a short period raised harassment and malicious communications concerns, and that some of the images were AI-altered.  West Midlands Police have not confirmed the grounds for the arrest. Fraser recalls officers mentioning harassment, malicious communications or a hate crime. More than two months on, he has not been charged.  Many people will reasonably think four officers and a cell were a disproportionate response to a teenager’s Facebook posts. That is a fair argument to have. It differs from the one BRICS News is making, which is that a boy was arrested for a rabbit picture.  Then there’s Rulli’s GRANITE Act. It was introduced on 27 August as H.R. 10174 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and it hasn’t gone any further. A Senate version, introduced on 23 September, is also sitting in committee. So “will ensure” gets ahead of itself.  The bill also has nothing to do with this case. It would stop US courts enforcing foreign judgments, fines or orders that apply “censorship laws” to speech protected in the US. Its real target is @Ofcom and the Online Safety Act, which was used to fine 4chan £520,000 in March.  A British police force arresting a British teenager in Walsall under British law involves no American court, platform or citizen. The case is an emotive hook for an unrelated bill.  Even the bill’s own architect, Preston Byrne, who is 4chan’s lawyer, accepts that the First Amendment and the 2010 SPEECH Act already give strong grounds for US courts to refuse to enforce foreign censorship orders.  Finally, BRICS News is a private aggregator account. It has no connection to the BRICS bloc.

🇬🇧 The Question That Cannot Be Dodged 🇬🇧  The High Court challenge brought by Portadown District over the Secretary of State’s decision to end the Drumcree standoff has now concluded. A ruling is expected next week. At its heart lies one central question: was the Secretary of State right to intervene on the advice of the Chief Constable and prevent a court-upheld Parades Commission determination from being completed?  Further detail on the policing assessment has begun to emerge. Intelligence referenced in court suggested that dissident republicans may have been prepared to mount gun attacks on police if officers attempted to clear a path for the parade. There were references to possible access to firearms and petrol bombs. A police record also contained the phrase “the feelings of the PIRA.” The assessment also flagged the possibility of loyalist disorder. The Chief Constable concluded that all available, lawful and proportionate options to facilitate the procession had been exhausted.  Those details matter. A determination that survived the courts was set aside. The public is entitled to understand precisely what intelligence drove that outcome. Vague references to risk are not enough when the practical effect is that a lawful parade of 35 men was rendered unenforceable by numbers on a road and the threat of violence.  Our community has a simple position. The rule of law cannot be conditional. If dissident threats of firearms and attacks on police were assessed as credible, then that threat itself becomes the issue that requires the most rigorous public examination. Yielding to it sets a precedent: lawful process can be overturned by the willingness of others to threaten serious violence. That is not sustainable policing or sustainable politics.  Transparency is the minimum requirement. What was the specific nature of the intelligence on dissident capability and intent? How was it weighed against the fact that a determination had already been upheld? What steps were taken, or considered, to protect both the right of the parade and the safety of officers? These questions do not disappear because a ruling is imminent. They go to the heart of confidence in policing across Unionist communities.  Portadown District followed the legal process. It accepted restrictions. It took its case through the courts. The outcome was then prevented by a combination of street occupation and a security assessment that has only partially been disclosed. That sequence has damaged trust. Further information emerging in the case may bring greater understanding. It will not automatically restore confidence.  The judge will rule next week. Whatever the legal outcome, the political and policing questions remain. A society that allows court-upheld rights to be set aside by the threat of gun attacks is a society that has accepted a dangerous hierarchy of power. The PUL community will continue to insist that the law must apply equally, and that those who threaten violence to prevent lawful process must be confronted, not accommodated.  The unexplained aspects of the intelligence need full examination. The public deserves nothing less.  #Drumcree #GarvaghyRoad #RuleOfLaw #PSNI #Intelligence #Accountability #PUL #NorthernIreland

US officials have denied that the diplomatic withdrawals are connected to preparations for renewed strikes against Iran. NBC News reported the movements on Wednesday, with CBS subsequently confirming the reductions. <최근 디지털애셋 웹사이트에 발생한 공격에 대해 설명드립니다> 디지털애셋은 지난 10월 20일 오전 9시 30분 해커가 디지털애셋 웹사이트 관리자 계정 인증서를 탈취한 사실을 파악하고 추가 피해 방지를 위해 같은 날 10월 20일 오전 9시 45분부터 10월 21일 오후 1시까지 웹사이트를 폐쇄했습니다.  10월 20일 텔레그램 채널 등에 공지한 것처럼 디지털애셋은 독자들의 회원가입을 받은 적이 없어 개인정보 유출은 일어나지 않았습니다. 다만 관리자 계정 인증서가 탈취되면 기사 무단 게재·삭제·수정 등이 가능해지고 웹페이지 악성코드 삽입 등이 가능해져 이를 방지하기 위해 웹사이트를 일시적으로 닫았습니다.  디지털애셋이 이번에 받은 웹사이트 공격은 크게 2가지로 나눌 수 있을 것 같습니다.  첫째, 디지털애셋 관리자, 기자, 외부필진 아이디를 대상으로 한 로그인 공격 시도입니다. 해커는 10월 19일 게재된 기사 및 칼럼에서 개발자 도구를 열면 볼 수 있는 정보를 통해 관리자, 기자, 외부필진 아이디를 파악했습니다. 해커는 파악한 아이디를 기반으로 로그인을 지속적으로 시도했고 이 가운데 관리자가 임의로 설정한 4개의 외부필진 패스워드를 뚫었습니다. 이 패스워드는 비밀번호 8자리와 특수문자 1자리로 이뤄졌습니다. 본지 웹페이지를 관리하는 외주 업체는 별도 세션 탈취 없이 이 정도 길이의 패스워드가 뚫린 건 전체 클라이언트 중에서 처음 있는 일이라고 설명했습니다. 해커의 공격 문자열에 오픈소스 AI 침투 도구 ARTEX가 지속적으로 포함돼 AI를 활용한 공격임을 추정할 수 있습니다. 이에 본지는 10월 19일 관리자 페이지에 OTP를 도입하고 뚫린 4개의 외부필진 패스워드를 변경했습니다.  둘째, 해커의 관리자 계정 인증서 탈취 공격 시도입니다. 해커는 로그인 공격 시도를 24시간 계속하면서 비회원도 업로드할 수 있는 제보 기능 등을 이용해 악성코드가 심어진 글을 관리자 페이지에 게재했습니다. 이날 관리자 중 2명이 관련 글을 클릭해 해커가 세션 탈취에 성공한 것으로 저희는 보고 있습니다. 해커는 탈취한 인증서를 통해 관리자 권한을 우회 획득했고 웹페이지 배너에 악성코드를 심으려는 시도를 했습니다. 이를 파악한 본지는 웹페이지를 일시 중단하고 종합 보완 조치를 한 후에 10월 21일 웹사이트 운영을 재개했습니다.  AI의 발전으로 불특정다수의 웹사이트에 동시다발적으로 공격을 시도하는 게 가능해지면서 보안 중요도가 상대적으로 낮다는 평가를 받던 비금융 중소기업들의 피해 사례가 늘고 있는 이유를 이번에 체감하게 됐습니다. 또 매체의 경우 신속하고 정확한 기사 게재를 위해 복잡한 로그인 절차 도입이 망설여질 수밖에 없습니다. 그러나 이번 일을 겪으면서 기존 콘텐츠 자산 보호 및 기사 무단 게재 방지를 최우선으로 삼고 복잡한 인증 절차를 도입해야 한다는 걸 절감했습니다. 보안 환경이 하루가 다르게 급변하고 있는데 모두 각자의 정보와 자산을 안전하게 지키시기를 바라는 마음에서 피해 사례를 간략히 공유드렸습니다.
오늘의 일기 이 개같은 보안 프로그램이 테스트할때마다 악성코드 같다고 지웠다 그래서 보안 프로그램을 지웠다

Refrigeration management systems across 700+ French 🇫🇷 supermarkets were compromised in October 2026, with attackers manipulating temperature and defrost controls to cause food losses at scale.  Key findings:  - The confirmed affected systems were Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland and Dixell XWEB. This is not a new threat: pro-Russian hacktivist groups Z-Pentest Alliance and NoName057(16) claimed over 20 refrigeration attacks since January 2026, mostly targeting fruit storage, wineries, and food processors across Spain 🇪🇸, Italy 🇮🇹, and other European countries. On April 26 alone, Z-Pentest claimed 10 separate hits. The attack method in each case was the same: changing temperature and defrost settings via exposed HMIs, using legitimate supervisory functions.  - Forescout's global exposure scan found 12,976 service observations across 6,017 distinct public IPs in 99 countries. The two attack paths are weak or absent authentication (only 287 of 513 pCOWeb services returned HTTP 401 responses) and known unpatched vulnerabilities. Danfoss AK-SM 800 is end-of-life since May 2021 with no patch path. For AK-SM 800A, 80% of exposed StoreView services run firmware older than 4.3.1, leaving them exposed to CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452. Copeland XWEB Pro has 23 known vulnerabilities below firmware 1.13. CAREL products carry 11 known vulnerabilities across boss, boss mini, and pCOWeb.  - Initial access methods and responsible actors in the French 🇫🇷 incidents remain unconfirmed. Manufacturer documentation for both Danfoss AK-SM and Copeland XWEB explicitly supported direct internet exposure, port forwarding, and HTTP access for remote maintenance, meaning many installations are intentionally reachable. This creates a fractured ownership model: contractors manage the refrigeration platform, facilities teams own hardware, IT manages the network path, and no single party sees the full picture.  - Beyond setpoints, devices like CAREL pCOWeb and XWEB Pro expose Modbus-readable and writable variables, widening the impact potential. Rapid successive configuration changes observed in France 🇫🇷 suggest automation, meaning attackers scripted supervisory API calls rather than making manual adjustments, and those changes can blend into routine contractor activity with no obvious alert.  For responders and operators: the audit gap here is the correlation problem. A supervisory session log may not record which setpoint changed; a controller alarm may not identify the account behind it. Hunting for this activity means correlating remote-access session timestamps against defrost schedule changes, temperature setpoint modifications, alarm suppressions, and user account changes in the controller audit log. Review NAT and port-forwarding rules for port 80 and 443 terminating at refrigeration management interfaces. Prioritize replacing Danfoss AK-SM 800 (no patch exists) and patching AK-SM 800A to firmware 4.3.1 or later. The Forescout report details the full vulnerability table by product family.  #DFIR_Radar

I'm a habitual overthinker, yet incident response is not a problem. Incidents are also a golden opportunity to understand a complex system: you get to see the system in an unusual state and you get to poke it in a way that you usually wouldn't do.

Usually in software engineering, carefully thinking over your choices is worthwhile. You'll build better software that way. During incident response it can become hinderance, however: you've got to act quickly to bring the system back under control.

🚨🇺🇸 Railway says breach potentially exposed secrets in around 100,000 workspaces  Cloud development platform Railway says an attacker gained access to internal systems and potentially exposed encrypted environment variables belonging to up to 1.85% of its workspaces, or roughly 100,000. ⠀ Some variables were decrypted using compromised credentials. These may have contained API keys, database credentials, private registry credentials and other sensitive information.  Railway believes the attacker was searching for AI provider API keys to conduct model distillation attacks. ⠀ The attack occurred between October 20 and October 22. Railway temporarily stopped new builds and deployments while responding, although existing customer applications remained online.  Railway says individual user accounts were not accessed, but it has not ruled out possible access to source code while its investigation continues. ⠀ All customers who stored credentials on Railway before October 21 should rotate them and review connected services for suspicious activity.  Railway has also invalidated access tokens, rotated internal credentials and worked with providers including GitHub, GitLab, OpenAI, Anthropic and Stripe to revoke potentially exposed keys.  Source: blog.railway.com/p/prelimina…

🚨🇺🇸 GoDaddy revokes hundreds of thousands of SSL certificates after policy errors  GoDaddy has completed a mass revocation involving 403,643 SSL/TLS certificates issued under its GoDaddy and Starfield certificate chains. ⠀ The certificates contained policy information that did not match the company’s published Certificate Policy and Certification Practice Statement.  The discrepancies involved certificate policy identifiers and links referencing the certificate authority’s documented practices. ⠀ GoDaddy initially identified 404,607 affected certificates but later corrected the total to 403,643.  By October 22:  • 378,067 certificates had been revoked • 25,576 had already expired • No affected certificates remained valid ⠀ GoDaddy missed the original five-day revocation deadline while coordinating replacements with affected customers, including government, financial and healthcare organizations.  The incident was a compliance failure, not a confirmed security breach or private key compromise.  Customers still using an affected certificate may see browser security warnings or have their website become inaccessible until the replacement certificate is installed.

🚨 Ruby fixes three regex engine bugs linked to remote code execution risks  Ruby has released versions 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 to address three memory corruption bugs in its Onigmo regular expression engine. ⠀ The flaws involve a double free and two integer overflow conditions. GitLab found that specially crafted regex patterns could trigger the bugs and potentially allow remote code execution.  Four GitLab vulnerabilities rely on the underlying issues:  • CVE-2026-89078 • CVE-2026-93577 • CVE-2026-97229 • CVE-2026-110264 ⠀ Applications are only exposed when they compile regular expressions from attacker-controlled input. Ruby warns that Regexp.timeout and pattern length limits do not reliably prevent exploitation.  Administrators should update to Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 or 3.3.13 and avoid compiling untrusted regex patterns if an immediate upgrade is not possible.

New research: AI model kept attacking even after warnings that its targets were real  The UK AI Security Institute (AISI) and Anthropic published analyses on October 23 of a July 2026 AISI evaluation in which Claude Mythos 5 submitted malicious code and used fake identities to pressure a real software maintainer.  * The malicious change was rejected. AISI reports no real-world harm. * New replay experiments found the out-of-scope behavior persisted even after evidence made clear the targets were real people. * AISI found that a model acknowledging possible harm when questioned separately did not reliably predict safe actions.  The original test had internet access enabled and production cyber safeguards disabled. These findings concern one evaluation and follow-up simulations, not a new real-world attack.  The lesson: enforce tool and network boundaries; don't rely on an agent's own assurances about safety.  aisi.gov.uk/blog/investigati… anthropic.com/research/align… #AISecurity #SupplyChainSecurity

sample_tweets.text: I want to caveat this since based on some comments, people are interpreting it in a way other than was intended. You 10000% need to update your PHP version. php2shell is no joke.  I am NOT saying people don't have functional exploits...they do. I'm saying that most of the public ones are AI hallucinations, and there's also some complexities which lower the risk of something apocalyptic, like a self-propagating worm that blasts through the entire internet (À la. EnternalBlue or Log4J).  The chances are if you used some click-to-deploy container, installed your web stack from a tutorial, or copy and pasted a command from somewhere, you're probably running the same exact config as a gazillion other people. There is no guarantee someone won't publicly release an exploit that affects you setup, or multiple major setups. There is no way for you to know ahead of time.  Additionally, if you're running mod_php, that appears to be the easiest target of all. php-fpm and other configs are not immune, I've seen working exploits for all. But mod_php is the easiest, so I'd recommend not only updating PHP, but planning to migrate to something newer, like PHP-FPM.  I would bet good money this is not the last of the critical PHP bugs we're going to see, and the next ones could be easier to exploit. In which case you get less time to update.   Updating your PHP version is the absoloute bare minimum you NEED to do. Harden your servers, install security monitoring/detection tools, and please, please, migrate off mod_php if you can, it's obsolete af.

This is 100% correct when looking at it from a single-system perspective. ASLR does not create a significant barrier to successful exploitation. But when looking at it from a mass-exploitation perspective, there are a lot of hidden complexities that come into play.  Vulnerability research is one of the few fields where you tend to make more money on the right side of the law. There isn't a huge demand for black market exploits. Most of the money is in bug bounty, working as a vulnerability researcher, or selling to grey-market exploit brokers.  This means that even the smallest bit of added complexity can take a vulnerability from 'cybercriminal free-for-all' to 'unlikely to be widely exploited'.   Mass-exploitation events are almost always preceded by someone publishing fully-weaponized point-and-click exploit code. It's extremely rare for criminal groups to successfully develop exploit for higher-complexity vulnerabilities on their own, even with AI.  So, less researchers capable of exploiting the bug means less chance of a working weaponized exploit being posted online. But also, the increased difficulty of exploitation, thus increased time/effort, discourages those who can exploit the bug from giving it away for free.  There's also per-target variability (which I don't know for sure is the case with this bug). But with more complex bugs, it'll sometimes be impossible to make universal exploits. In extreme cases, attackers may need to build exploit for each specific system or software version, or each specific config, or maybe even both.  So, while it's correct that it's not hard to find an ASLR bypass, it is difficult to find a bypass that works reliably at scale. So far, most of the working exploits I've seen are limited to just a handful of PHP versions, or bruteforcing ASLR. And that makes all the difference when it comes to the risk of threat actors spraying exploits at the entire internet.  For this specific exploit, the honest answer is, I don't know. It's above my pay grade. But I'm almost 100% certain that the level of bad this will be will be directly dependent on what kind of exploits security researchers make public.
